title: Pathology - Intermediate Fundamentals
description: Pathology fundamentals covering cellular injury, inflammation, neoplasia, and disease mechanisms for medical students.

questions.explanation: Pathology is the study of disease, including causes (etiology), mechanisms (pathogenesis), and effects on the body.

answers.answer_text: The study of disease, its causes, mechanisms, and effects
The study of normal body functions

questions.explanation: Necrosis is pathological cell death caused by external factors (ischemia, toxins, infection), triggering inflammation.

answers.answer_text: Pathological cell death due to injury, causing inflammation

questions.explanation: Apoptosis is programmed cell death - orderly, controlled, no inflammation. Important in development and homeostasis.

questions.question_text: What are the cardinal signs of inflammation?
questions.explanation: The five cardinal signs are: Rubor (redness), Calor (heat), Tumor (swelling), Dolor (pain), Functio laesa (loss of function).

answers.answer_text: Redness, heat, swelling, pain, loss of function

questions.question_text: What is the difference between acute and chronic inflammation?
questions.explanation: Acute: rapid onset, neutrophils, short duration. Chronic: prolonged, lymphocytes/macrophages, tissue destruction and repair.

answers.answer_text: Acute is rapid with neutrophils; chronic is prolonged with lymphocytes/macrophages
Acute lasts years; chronic is brief
Acute only affects skin; chronic affects organs

questions.explanation: Hypertrophy is an increase in cell SIZE (not number) due to increased workload or hormonal stimulation.
Hyperplasia is an increase in cell NUMBER, often in response to hormones or growth factors.
Atrophy is a decrease in cell size or number, often due to disuse, denervation, or decreased blood supply.

answers.answer_text: Decrease in cell size or number

questions.explanation: Metaplasia is reversible replacement of one mature cell type with another (e.g., respiratory epithelium to squamous in smokers).

answers.answer_text: Reversible change of one cell type to another

questions.explanation: Dysplasia is disordered cell growth with abnormal size, shape, and organization - a precancerous change.

questions.question_text: What is the difference between benign and malignant tumors?
questions.explanation: Benign: well-differentiated, localized, no metastasis. Malignant: poorly differentiated, invasive, can metastasize.

answers.answer_text: Benign is localized and doesn't spread; malignant invades and metastasizes
Benign is always fatal; malignant is not

questions.explanation: Coagulative necrosis preserves cell outlines (denatured proteins); typical of ischemic injury (except brain).

answers.answer_text: Necrosis that preserves cell structure, typical of ischemia
Necrosis seen only in the brain

questions.explanation: Liquefactive necrosis involves enzymatic digestion of tissue, forming liquid; seen in brain infarcts and bacterial infections.

answers.answer_text: Necrosis with enzymatic digestion creating liquid; seen in brain and abscesses

questions.explanation: Caseous necrosis has a cheese-like appearance; characteristic of tuberculosis and some fungal infections.
An embolus is any intravascular material (thrombus, fat, air, tumor) that travels and lodges in a vessel.

answers.answer_text: Intravascular material that travels and blocks a vessel downstream
A blood clot that stays in place

questions.explanation: A thrombus is a blood clot that forms in a vessel or heart chamber and remains attached to the vessel wall.

answers.answer_text: A blood clot that forms and remains attached in a blood vessel

questions.explanation: Virchow's triad: Endothelial injury, Stasis/turbulence, Hypercoagulability - factors predisposing to thrombosis.
Edema is abnormal accumulation of fluid in interstitial spaces or body cavities.

questions.question_text: What is the main cell type in acute inflammation?
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are the first cells to arrive at sites of acute inflammation (first responders).
Granulomatous inflammation features granulomas (aggregates of macrophages/epithelioid cells); seen in TB, sarcoidosis.

answers.answer_text: Chronic inflammation with collections of activated macrophages (granulomas)

questions.question_text: What is the hallmark of type I hypersensitivity?
questions.explanation: Type I hypersensitivity is IgE-mediated with mast cell degranulation; includes anaphylaxis, allergies, asthma.
An infarct is an area of ischemic necrosis caused by occlusion of arterial supply or venous drainage.

answers.answer_text: Area of tissue death due to ischemia (blocked blood supply)

questions.explanation: Tumor suppressor genes (e.g., p53, Rb) normally inhibit cell proliferation; their loss contributes to cancer.

answers.answer_text: Genes that normally inhibit cell growth; loss contributes to cancer

questions.explanation: Oncogenes are mutated/overexpressed genes that promote cell proliferation and contribute to cancer development.

answers.answer_text: Genes that promote cell growth and can cause cancer when activated

questions.question_text: What is the function of p53?
questions.explanation: p53 is the 'guardian of the genome' - it arrests cell cycle and triggers apoptosis in damaged cells. Most commonly mutated gene in cancer.

answers.answer_text: Arrests cell cycle and induces apoptosis in damaged cells
